beliefs.origin: new (rule 4 model). Counts only people who had been dependent and were fully free at the first interview (1,772 re-interviewed). A survey, not a trial: people chose to drink lightly or not at all.

windows.label: Shaky, sweaty, anxious, bad sleep
windows.when: From hour 6 after the last drink; often gone in 2–7 days
windows.changeNote: rev2: was '6–36 hours', e 36: the source checker found it more hopeful than the page's own 2-7 days card, and ASAM's 36 h is how long mild cases are watched, not when shakes stop. ASAM: 'Signs and symptoms of alcohol withdrawal typically begin 6–24 hours after cessation of (or reduction in) alcohol use.' Mirijello 2015 (r18, to add to the research refs): 'The mild-moderate form of AWS is often self-managed by patients or disappears within 2–7 days from the last drink'. Label and peak unchanged.

windows.label: Seizure risk, if you drank heavily every day
Deep confusion, seeing things (the DTs)
windows.when: About 5 in 100 people with withdrawal; usually starts day 2–4, can start as late as day 10; seeing things alone can start at hour 12
windows.changeNote: rev2: was 'Day 2–7, rare' with no source for 'rare' (source checker); 'DTs' alone was jargon (cold readers). Mirijello 2015 (r18): 'Delirium tremens … occurrs approximately in 5% of patients with AWS'. ASAM (r1): 'Hallucinations develop within 12–24 hours following cessation of (or reduction in) alcohol use'. Start, peak and end unchanged.

windows.label: Irritable, anxious, poor sleep
windows.when: From day 5–7, for weeks, sometimes months
windows.changeNote: rev2: was 'Day 5 to several weeks'; ASAM gives no start day (source checker) and cold readers saw a clash with the 2-7 days card. Mirijello 2015 (r18): 'some symptoms can persist from weeks to months following the 5–7 days of acute detoxification period'. ASAM (r1): 'subacute symptoms of irritability, anxiety and sleep disturbances can persist for weeks'. Start, end and open end unchanged.

windows.label: Less pleasure in things
windows.when: Seen in some people up to a year

windows.label: Light, broken sleep, slowly mending
windows.when: Falling asleep normal by month 5–9; total sleep back in 1–2 years; broken sleep can last 1–3 years
windows.changeNote: rev2: was 'full repair 1–2 years', e 17520: the source checker found it more hopeful than Brower 2001 (r13), where only total sleep time takes 1-2 years and broken sleep lasts longer. Brower: 'sleep fragmentation manifested by increases in sleep-stage changes, brief arousals, and REM sleep disruptions can persist for 1 to 3 years after establishing sobriety'. 'total sleep time took 1 to 2 years to return to normal levels'. End now 3 years; fall kept.

do: Don’t stop yet. This week, drink as you normally do, and watch it.
Already stopped? Don’t start drinking again to do this step: write it from memory.
Write down what drinking does for you: unwinding, sleep, confidence, fun with friends.
Before each drink, note the time, the place and what you want from it. Next morning, note whether you got it.
Allow it. No guilt and no promises this week. You’re finding out, not judging.
Look at each reason up close: does drinking give you that, or take it back by morning?
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the beliefs above.
plan.editNote: 2026-11-06: plan action edited after the round-2 safety audit (no new figure, no source change)

do: Unwinding: a walk, a shower, a hard workout, a show.
Going out: an alcohol-free beer in your hand, ordered first, before anyone asks.
Friends: see the ones you’d enjoy sober; meet them for food, sport or coffee.
Sleep: same bedtime every night, a hot shower, no phone in bed. Expect light sleep at first; it mends slowly, over months to years.
Confidence: arrive early, before the room fills, and start one conversation while you’re fresh.
Home: keep a cold soft drink you like in the fridge for the hour you’d pour one.
Clear the house of drink the day before.
Drinking heavily every day, or get the shakes when you stop? Stop with a doctor, not alone.
Tell one person the date.
Plan every Friday for the first two months: where you’ll be, and what you’ll drink instead.
One thing only: no new diet and no other big change for these three months. A walk or a workout as a swap is fine.
Slip? Don’t wait for Monday, and don’t go back to days of normal drinking: the same day, ask what that drink gave you.

do: When “just one” comes, answer the way a non-drinker would: “I don’t drink.”
When the urge comes, name it: “there is a craving.” Not “I want a drink.” Not “I need one.”
Then watch it like weather. Notice when it peaks and when it fades.
Feel fine and think “maybe it wasn’t that bad”? That’s the quitting working, not proof you never had to.
Unsure what to do? Ask what the man a year sober would do tonight, and do that.
Count the mornings you wake up clear, not the days you missed.
Ask a doctor about acamprosate or naltrexone, two prescription pills that help people stay stopped.
Try AA or another group that meets weekly.
Use help as a tool for a stretch, not a new identity. Keep what works, drop the rest.
Ask one friend to check in with you on Fridays for the first two months.
Slipped more than once? Add one kind of help you haven’t tried, and ask step 1’s questions again the same day, not after days of normal drinking.

proof.text: In trials, some reported by its maker, 36 in 100 people hooked on alcohol, after detox, stayed fully off drink six months on acamprosate; 23 in 100 on a dummy pill. The best-run trials showed a small, unclear gap.
